exam: What sterilisation method would you choose for a heat‑sensitive endoscope in a district hospital? — Explain why moist heat is unsuitable, discuss glutaraldehyde immersion with required exposure time, and note monitoring requirements.

A patient develops a surgical site infection 3 days after an operation; the autoclave log shows a ‘pass’ but the biological indicator was not used. What should you do? — Highlight need for a repeat cycle, environmental cultures, and empirical antibiotics.

How does sterilisation differ from high‑level disinfection, and why is this distinction clinically important? — Define each, note that spores survive high‑level disinfection, and relate to risk of SSI.

In a low‑resource clinic without an autoclave, how can you ensure instrument sterility for minor procedures? — Discuss chemical sterilants, proper concentration, exposure time, and use of boiled water as adjunct.

What are the consequences of using a sterilisation method that does not achieve the required temperature, and how would you detect this failure? — Explain residual viable spores, use of biological indicators, and visual cues of inadequate steam.

During a sterilisation audit, you find that instrument packs are damp after the cycle. What does this indicate and how should you act? — Dampness suggests incomplete drying, risk of microbial survival; recommend re‑run cycle or improve drying phase.

Why are prions resistant to standard sterilisation, and what additional steps are required for neurosurgical instruments? — Mention prion resistance to heat, need for extended autoclave cycles or sodium hydroxide treatment.

A hospital experiences an outbreak of catheter‑related bloodstream infections. How would you investigate the role of sterilisation? — Review sterilisation logs, indicator results, culture catheter hubs, and assess reprocessing technique.
ai.title: Sterilisation in Clinical Practice
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Sterilisation eliminates all viable microorganisms. Understanding methods, indications, and limitations is vital for infection control, especially where resources are limited.

b: Essential for surgical instruments, implants, and critical care equipment.
In low‑resource settings, choice of method balances efficacy, cost, and availability.
sections.p: Sterilisation is the complete destruction or removal of all forms of microbial life, including bacterial spores. It differs from disinfection, which may leave spores viable.

t.a: Physical method availability (e.g., autoclave, dry heat)
t.b: Can the facility achieve required temperature/time? – If not, consider chemical sterilisation or referral.

b: Moist heat (steam) at 121 °C for 15 min under 15 psi is standard.
Chemical agents (e.g., glutaraldehyde) need ≥20 min immersion for high‑level disinfection; true sterilisation may need longer exposure.
sections.p: Effective sterilisation must reach conditions that inactivate the most resistant organisms (e.g., bacterial spores, prions). Key parameters are temperature, pressure, time, and moisture.

t.b: Has sterilisation succeeded? – Growth indicates failure; no growth confirms efficacy.

b: Critical items (surgical tools, endoscopes) must be sterilised before each use.
Semi‑critical items (laryngoscope blades) may be high‑level disinfected if sterilisation not feasible.
sections.p: Sterilisation interrupts the chain of infection by removing the source of pathogens from medical devices, preventing patient‑to‑patient spread.

b: SSIs increase morbidity, length of stay, and mortality, especially in trauma and obstetric surgery.
In low‑resource hospitals, outbreaks often trace to inadequate instrument sterilisation.
sections.p: Proper sterilisation prevents device‑associated infections such as surgical site infection (SSI), catheter‑related bloodstream infection, and prion disease transmission.

b: Review sterilisation logs, indicator results, and equipment maintenance records.
Consider environmental cultures if outbreak suspected.
sections.p: When infection occurs despite presumed sterile technique, assess sterilisation process and look for breaches.

t.b: Is there contamination of the sterilisation area? – Positive growth suggests process failure.

b: Empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics pending cultures; de‑escalate based on sensitivities.
Train staff on proper cleaning, packaging, and cycle monitoring.
sections.p: Management focuses on source control, appropriate antimicrobial therapy, and reinforcement of sterilisation protocols.

t.b: Which pathogen is causing the infection? – Guides targeted therapy.

b: Moist heat is preferred for heat‑stable instruments; chemical sterilants for heat‑sensitive equipment.
A failed biological indicator mandates repeat cycle and investigation of cause.
In resource‑limited settings, validate chemical sterilisation with exposure time and concentration checks.
sections.p: Key points examiners test: distinction between sterilisation and disinfection, appropriate method selection, interpretation of indicator results, and steps when sterilisation fails.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly spreading surgical site infection with systemic signs (fever, hypotension) – urgent surgical review and infection control involvement.
